t: Overflow a stack buffer and redirect execution to win() (ret2win)
desc: On a non-PIE 64-bit lab binary with a gets()/read() into a fixed buffer, overflow the saved return address so control jumps to a win()/print_flag() function. Watch 16-byte stack alignment.
check: Running your exploit makes the program print the flag via win()
You can state the exact byte offset from buffer start to the saved return address
Your payload includes a ret padding gadget when needed to fix movaps stack alignment

t: Find the exact saved-RIP offset with a cyclic De Bruijn pattern
desc: Feed a pwntools cyclic() pattern into a crashing binary, read the faulting address in GDB/core, and use cyclic_find() to compute the precise overflow offset to the return address.
check: You derive the offset to saved RIP in a single crash, not by brute force
cyclic_find on the leaked value matches the offset you then use successfully
Your notes explain why a 4-byte pattern slice maps to a unique position

t: Master the x86-64 System V integer calling convention
desc: Learn how the first six integer/pointer arguments and the return value are passed in registers, and why this matters for building ROP calls to functions like system().
check: Which registers hold the first six integer arguments, in order?
Where is a function's integer return value placed, and who cleans the stack?
Why does a ret2libc call to system("/bin/sh") need a pop rdi; ret gadget?
a: rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9; further args go on the stack right-to-left.
In rax. Under SysV the caller cleans up stack-passed args (callee-cleanup is not used).
Because the "/bin/sh" pointer must be in rdi before the call, so you load rdi via the gadget.

t: Leak libc with puts(GOT), then ret2libc to spawn a shell
desc: On a dynamically linked NX binary, build a ROP chain that calls puts on puts@GOT to leak its runtime address, returns to main, computes libc base, then calls system("/bin/sh").
check: Your exploit prints a shell even though libc is ASLR-randomized
The leaked puts address minus the known libc offset gives a page-aligned base
You explain why returning to main (or _start) lets you send a second-stage payload

t: Build a ROP chain to call execve("/bin/sh",0,0) in a static binary
desc: With no libc import to abuse, use a gadget finder (ROPgadget/ropper) on a statically linked binary to set rax=59, rdi->"/bin/sh", rsi=rdx=0, then syscall.
check: Your chain runs execve and drops to a shell with NX enabled
You locate or write the "/bin/sh" string into writable memory and point rdi at it
You can name every register the execve syscall reads and the syscall number

t: Understand stack canaries and the ways they are bypassed
desc: Learn how the compiler places and checks a stack canary, where the value comes from, and the main strategies attackers use to defeat it.
check: Where is the canary stored relative to local buffers and the saved return address, and when is it checked?
Why does the canary's least-significant byte conventionally being 0x00 both help and hinder attackers?
Name two ways to exploit a vulnerable function without ever corrupting the canary.
a: Between the local buffers and saved RBP/RIP; it is validated just before ret, calling __stack_chk_fail on mismatch.
The null byte stops string functions from leaking it, but also terminates attacker strings/leaks at that byte.
Leak the canary first then include it in the payload; or overwrite non-return targets (GOT, func pointers) without passing the canary.

t: Leak a stack canary with a format string, then overflow to win()
desc: Use a printf format-string bug to leak the canary off the stack with a positional %p, then in a second input overflow the buffer, replace the canary with the leaked value, and overwrite RIP with win().
check: The binary reaches win() without triggering __stack_chk_fail
The value you leak ends in a null byte, confirming it is the canary
You identify the correct %N$p index that lands on the canary slot

t: Use a format-string bug to leak stack values and find your input offset
desc: Send a controlled printf format like AAAA.%p.%p.%p... (or %N$p) to a vulnerable program and determine which positional argument index corresponds to your own input on the stack.
check: You print 0x41414141 (or 0x4141414141414141) proving you found your input's index
You can read an arbitrary stack slot with a single %N$p
You note the difference in argument consumption between 32-bit and 64-bit here

t: Overwrite a GOT entry with a format-string %n write
desc: On a Partial-RELRO binary, use %n/%hn with width specifiers to write the address of win() (or system) over a GOT entry such as printf/exit, so the next call redirects.
check: Calling the hijacked function transfers control to your target
You split the write into two %hn halves to avoid printing billions of bytes
You confirm Full RELRO would have blocked this and explain why

t: Understand GOT/PLT lazy binding and why GOT overwrites work
desc: Learn how calls to shared-library functions route through the PLT and GOT, how the dynamic linker resolves them on first use, and what RELRO changes.
check: Walk through what happens the first time a program calls puts@plt versus later calls.
Why does overwriting a GOT entry hijack control flow on the next call?
How do Partial RELRO and Full RELRO each change the exploitability of the GOT?
a: First call goes PLT -> GOT -> dynamic resolver, which writes the real address into the GOT; later calls jump straight to it via the GOT.
Because the PLT reads the target from the GOT each call, so a forged GOT entry sends the call to attacker-chosen code.
Partial RELRO leaves the GOT writable (overwrite works); Full RELRO resolves at load and makes the GOT read-only, blocking it.

t: Use ret2csu to control rdx when gadgets are scarce
desc: Leverage the __libc_csu_init universal gadgets to populate rdx/rsi/rdi and call a function through a pointer, enabling calls that need a third argument in a gadget-poor binary.
check: Your chain sets rdx to a chosen value and makes a controlled call
You correctly account for the pop rbx/rbp/r12-r15 sequence and the loop's add rbx,1 compare
You explain why ret2csu is useful when no clean pop rdx; ret gadget exists

t: Defeat PIE with a partial return-address overwrite
desc: On a PIE binary where you can overwrite only the low bytes of the saved return address, redirect execution to a nearby function/gadget within the same page without knowing the full base.
check: You redirect control by rewriting only 1-2 low bytes of saved RIP
Your target lies within the bytes that are not randomized by page alignment
You explain why the lowest 12 bits (3 hex nibbles) are fixed under 4KB-page ASLR

t: Understand what ASLR randomizes and how one leak defeats it
desc: Learn which memory regions ASLR randomizes, what it leaves fixed, and why leaking a single pointer into a module collapses the whole randomization for that module.
check: Which regions does ASLR randomize, and what stays at a fixed address in a non-PIE binary?
If you leak one libc function's runtime address, how do you compute the base of libc?
Why does page alignment mean the low 12 bits of an address are not secret?
a: Stack, heap, mmap/shared libraries, and the PIE base; a non-PIE executable's own image stays at its fixed link address.
Subtract that function's known file offset within libc from the leaked address to get the page-aligned base.
mmap/segment bases are page-aligned (4KB), so the bottom 12 bits come from the fixed in-file offset, not randomization.

t: Poison a tcache fd pointer to get an arbitrary malloc chunk
desc: On a glibc ~2.31 heap challenge with a use-after-free or overflow, corrupt a freed tcache chunk's fd pointer so a subsequent malloc returns an attacker-chosen address (e.g. over a function pointer or __free_hook).
check: A later malloc returns a pointer to your target address
You account for the tcache count field so the allocator hands back your chunk
You explain how this differs on glibc 2.32+ due to safe-linking pointer mangling

t: Understand the glibc tcache: binning, reuse, and double-free checks
desc: Learn how per-thread tcache bins store freed chunks, how allocation reuses them, and what double-free protection was added across glibc versions.
check: How are freed chunks organized in the tcache and in what order are they handed back?
What is the default maximum number of chunks per tcache bin, and what selects a bin?
What check did glibc 2.29 add against tcache double-free, and how does safe-linking (2.32) differ?
a: In per-thread singly linked LIFO bins keyed by request size; malloc pops the most recently freed chunk first.
Seven chunks per bin by default (tcache_count), with one bin per small size class.
2.29 added a per-chunk key field checked on free to catch double-frees; 2.32 added safe-linking, XOR-mangling fd pointers with the chunk's address.

t: Understand NX/DEP and why return-oriented programming exists
desc: Learn how the no-execute bit stops classic shellcode injection and why reusing existing executable code (ROP) is the standard response, contrasted with ret2shellcode.
check: What does the NX bit enforce on the stack and heap, and what attack does it stop?
Why can a ROP chain still run arbitrary logic despite W^X?
In what situation is ret2shellcode viable instead of ROP?
a: It marks data pages (stack/heap) non-executable, so injected shellcode on them faults instead of running.
ROP chains short existing instruction sequences ending in ret, performing computation using only already-executable code.
When a region is both writable and executable (NX disabled or an RWX mapping), you can jump to injected shellcode directly.

t: Inject and run shellcode on a stack with NX disabled
desc: Compile a lab binary with an executable stack (or use one provided), generate shellcode with pwntools shellcraft, place it in the buffer, and overwrite RIP to jump to it.
check: The program executes your shellcode and gives a shell
You jump to the correct in-memory address of your shellcode (leak or jmp rsp style)
You confirm the stack is executable (checksec / readelf GNU_STACK)

t: Pop a shell with a one_gadget given a libc leak
desc: Run the one_gadget tool against the target libc, pick a magic gadget, satisfy its register/stack constraints, and jump to libc_base + gadget offset to exec /bin/sh in a single hop.
check: Jumping to your chosen one_gadget yields a shell
You verified the gadget's constraints (e.g. rsi/rdx NULL) actually hold at jump time
You can explain why one_gadget is shorter than a full system("/bin/sh") chain

t: Understand integer bugs that turn into buffer overflows
desc: Learn how signed/unsigned confusion and integer truncation/overflow let a length check pass while a copy writes far more than the buffer holds.
check: How can a negative signed length defeat a bounds check and still cause a huge memcpy?
What happens when a 16-bit length counter wraps while the real data is larger?
Why is comparing a signed length against a buffer size with < dangerous?
a: A negative int passes an "if (len < size)" check but is reinterpreted as a huge size_t by memcpy, copying far too much.
The counter wraps to a small value so the check passes, yet the loop/copy still processes the full oversized input.
An attacker-controlled negative value is < size as signed but becomes enormous once widened to unsigned for the copy.

t: Pivot the stack with leave;ret to run a longer ROP chain
desc: When the overflow only gives you a few bytes past RIP, use a leave;ret or pop rsp gadget to move rsp into a buffer you fully control (e.g. a bss/read area) and continue a larger chain there.
check: Execution continues into your relocated chain and reaches the final goal
rsp lands exactly at the start of your staged chain after the pivot
You explain how leave (mov rsp,rbp; pop rbp) enables the pivot when you control saved RBP
